# Chapter 32 — Low-Power RTL Design & Power-Aware Verification

*Engineering & Verifying Power Management in Modern Digital Systems*

> "Power is no longer a post-implementation concern. It is an architectural constraint that shapes every design decision — and every verification decision."

## Chapter Objective

Modern chips must manage power aggressively — mobile, automotive, IoT, AI, and data-center applications all impose strict energy budgets. This chapter covers power domains, UPF/CPF, clock gating, power gating, retention, isolation, level shifting, always-on logic, power sequencing, and power-aware verification using simulation and formal methods.

## 32.1 Why Power Management Matters

Power directly affects battery life, thermal performance, reliability, cooling cost, and regulatory compliance. Low-power failures cause incorrect initialization, data corruption, functional failure, and system instability.

## 32.2 Power Domains

A power domain groups logic sharing a common power supply that can be switched together:

```text
Always-On Domain → CPU Domain → GPU Domain → DDR Domain →
Peripheral Domain → Ultra-Low-Power Domain
```

Each domain may be independently powered, gated, retained, or shut down.

## 32.3 UPF & CPF

**UPF** (Unified Power Format, IEEE 1801) and **CPF** (Common Power Format) describe power intent in a format consumed by synthesis, simulation, and formal tools. Verification uses UPF/CPF to simulate power-state behavior.

## 32.4 Power States

```text
Active → Idle → Clock-Gated → Retention → Power-Down → Off
```

Each transition must be verified — both the transition itself and recovery from it.

## 32.5 Clock Gating

Disables the clock to unused logic, reducing dynamic power without losing state. Types: integrated clock gating (ICG), enable-based, hierarchical.

```text
Enable → ICG → Gated Clock → Registers
```

Verification: correct enable timing, glitch-free clock gating, wake-up behavior, interaction with reset.

## 32.6 Power Gating

Completely removes power from a domain — maximum power saving but state is lost:

```text
Isolate → Retain → Gate Power → [Powered Down] →
Restore Power → Release Retention → Release Isolation → Resume
```

Verification: correct sequence, isolation correctness, retention correctness, recovery.

## 32.7 Isolation Cells

Prevent undefined values from a powered-down domain driving active logic. Isolation value (0 or 1) must be set before power-down. Verification: assertion timing, release timing, correct isolation value, protocol impact.

## 32.8 Retention Registers

Special registers that preserve state during power gating using a separate always-on supply. Verification: save operation, state preserved during power-down, restore operation, correctness after restore.

## 32.9 Level Shifters

Translate signals between domains operating at different supply voltages. Missing or incorrect level shifters cause signal integrity failures. Verification: correct voltage levels, directionality, power-state interaction.

## 32.10 Always-On (AO) Domain

Logic that remains powered in all power states: power management controller, wakeup logic, RTC, security monitor. Always-on signals that drive power-gated domains require isolation. Verification: AO functionality during all power states, isolation from gated domains.

## 32.11 Power Sequencing

```text
Power-Down: Isolate → Save → Gate Clock → Remove Power
Power-Up:   Apply Power → Enable Clock → Restore → Release Isolation
```

Incorrect sequencing causes data corruption, latch-up, or functional failure. Verification must exercise every sequence variant.

## 32.12 Wakeup Latency

Time from wakeup event to operational state. Verification: minimum and maximum latency, wakeup during active traffic, multiple wakeup sources.

## 32.13 Power-Aware Simulation

UPF/CPF-aware simulators model power intent directly — power state propagation, isolation behavior, retention behavior, level shifting, and undefined values during power transitions. This extends standard RTL simulation with power-state awareness.

## 32.14 Voltage Islands

Different functional blocks operating at different supply voltages for performance and power trade-offs. Verification: level shifter correctness, interface behavior during voltage changes, safety during transitions.

## 32.15 Dynamic Voltage & Frequency Scaling (DVFS)

Adjusts voltage and frequency together for workload-matched efficiency. Verification: correct voltage-frequency pairs, transition behavior, performance and correctness under all operating points.

## 32.16 Power Management Controller (PMC)

Controls power sequencing, wakeup, retention, isolation, and power states. The PMC is one of the highest-risk blocks to verify because errors affect the entire chip.

## 32.17 Verification Strategy

```text
Power State Identification → Transition Mapping → Sequence Planning →
Clock Gating Tests → Power Gating Tests → Retention Tests →
Wakeup Tests → DVFS Tests → Stress Tests → Formal Verification → Signoff
```

## 32.18 Directed Tests

Clock gate enable/disable, power gate sequence, retention save/restore, isolation cell behavior, wakeup from each power state, DVFS operating point transitions. Directed tests establish correct behavior per scenario.

## 32.19 Constrained-Random Verification

Randomize power state sequences, wakeup sources, traffic during transitions, retention scenarios, and DVFS operating points. CRV exposes unexpected interactions between power management and functional logic.

## 32.20 Assertions

Isolation before power-down, retention save before power removal, correct power-up sequence, no uninitialized values in active domain, correct level-shifter behavior, wakeup completion.

## 32.21 Functional Coverage

Power states, power transitions, power-state combinations, retention save/restore, isolation scenarios, wakeup sources, DVFS operating points. Coverage ensures all power management scenarios are exercised.

## 32.22 Formal Verification

Particularly valuable for power sequencing: prove correct isolation order, retention correctness, no undefined propagation, safe wakeup. Formal complements simulation by proving properties exhaustively.

## 32.23 Common Low-Power Bugs

Missing isolation, incorrect isolation value, incorrect power sequence, retention failure, level-shifter absence, wakeup timeout, power domain interaction, reset during power transition, DVFS operating-point error. Common sources of silicon power failures.

## 32.24 Debug Methodology

```text
Power Failure → Identify Power Domain → Check Sequence →
Check Isolation → Check Retention → Check Level Shifters →
Check PMC → Root Cause
```

Power failures often manifest as data corruption or unexpected reset — always inspect power sequencing first.

## 32.25 Power Signoff Checklist

UPF/CPF reviewed, all power domains documented, isolation verified, retention verified, level shifters verified, power sequencing verified, wakeup verified, DVFS verified, formal verification complete, coverage closed, waivers approved.

## 32.26 Best Practices

Define UPF/CPF early and keep it synchronized with RTL; verify isolation before retention before gating; test every power-state transition; include power transitions in regression; use formal tools to prove sequencing properties; measure wakeup latency under realistic conditions; review power management controller thoroughly.

## 32.27 Chapter Summary

Low-power design is a first-class engineering discipline, not a post-implementation consideration. Professional verification engineers must understand power domains, UPF/CPF, clock gating, power gating, retention, isolation, level shifting, DVFS, power sequencing, and the comprehensive verification strategy required to demonstrate correct behavior across all power states and transitions.

## Engineering Exercise

For a mobile SoC with five power domains: (1) draw the power architecture; (2) define all power states; (3) map all power transitions; (4) identify isolation requirements; (5) verify correct power sequences; (6) test retention save/restore; (7) verify level shifters; (8) test wakeup from each power state; (9) write assertions for sequencing and isolation; (10) produce a power signoff report.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**Power management bugs are among the most expensive to diagnose because they produce symptoms far removed from their cause — data corruption from missing isolation, initialization failure from incorrect sequencing, and intermittent behavior from retention errors. Verify the power architecture as rigorously as the functional architecture.**

# Chapter 33 — Parameterized RTL & Generate Constructs

*Designing & Verifying Scalable, Reusable Hardware Architectures*

> "Parameterized RTL solves the same problem once. Non-parameterized RTL solves it again, differently, every time."

## Chapter Objective

Professional RTL is parameterized — data widths, address widths, FIFO depths, pipeline stages, channel counts, and bus widths are defined by parameters rather than constants. Generate constructs create scalable hardware structures from those parameters. This chapter covers parameterization philosophy, parameter types, generate loops, generate conditionals, verification of parameterized designs, configuration coverage, and common bugs.

## 33.1 Why Parameterization Matters

Hard-coded RTL requires manual changes for every new configuration — error-prone, expensive to maintain, and difficult to reuse. Parameterized RTL supports any legal configuration from a single implementation.

## 33.2 Parameters vs. Localparams

**Parameters** are configurable from outside the module — set at instantiation.
**Localparams** are internal constants — calculated from parameters, not overridable.

```systemverilog
module axi_fifo #(
    parameter DATA_WIDTH  = 32,
    parameter ADDR_WIDTH  = 8,
    parameter FIFO_DEPTH  = 256
)(
    input  logic                  clk,
    input  logic                  rst_n,
    input  logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] wdata,
    output logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] rdata
);
    localparam PTR_WIDTH = $clog2(FIFO_DEPTH);
```

## 33.3 Common Parameter Types

Data width, address width, ID width, burst length, FIFO depth, pipeline stages, channel count, bus width, memory size, cache ways and sets, priority levels, timeout values.

## 33.4 Parameter Validation

Always validate parameters at elaboration time:

```systemverilog
initial begin
    if (DATA_WIDTH < 8 || DATA_WIDTH > 1024)
        $fatal(1, "DATA_WIDTH must be between 8 and 1024");
    if ((FIFO_DEPTH & (FIFO_DEPTH - 1)) != 0)
        $fatal(1, "FIFO_DEPTH must be a power of two");
end
```

Validation prevents difficult-to-debug elaboration errors.

## 33.5 Generate Loops

Create multiple hardware instances from a single template:

```systemverilog
generate
    for (genvar i = 0; i < NUM_CHANNELS; i++) begin : gen_channel
        axi_channel #(.DATA_WIDTH(DATA_WIDTH)) u_ch (
            .clk   (clk),
            .rst_n (rst_n),
            .data  (data[i])
        );
    end
endgenerate
```

Generate loops create synthesizable, parameterizable hardware arrays.

## 33.6 Generate Conditionals

Select between hardware implementations based on parameters:

```systemverilog
generate
    if (USE_ECC) begin : gen_ecc
        ecc_engine u_ecc (.data(data), .syndrome(syndrome));
    end else begin : gen_no_ecc
        assign syndrome = '0;
    end
endgenerate
```

Generate conditionals allow a single RTL file to support multiple hardware configurations.

## 33.7 Hierarchical Generate

Generate blocks may be nested — an outer loop across channels, an inner conditional per channel based on its index. Verification must understand the generated hierarchy.

## 33.8 `$clog2` Usage

```systemverilog
localparam PTR_WIDTH = $clog2(FIFO_DEPTH);  // pointer bit width
localparam ADDR_BITS = $clog2(MEM_DEPTH);   // address bit width
```

A common source of off-by-one errors — verify that `$clog2` results are correct at boundary values (power-of-two and non-power-of-two depths).

## 33.9 Parameterized Interfaces

SystemVerilog interfaces can be parameterized for scalable, reusable testbench connectivity:

```systemverilog
interface axi_if #(parameter DATA_WIDTH = 32, parameter ADDR_WIDTH = 32) (
    input logic clk, input logic rst_n
);
    logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] wdata;
    logic [ADDR_WIDTH-1:0] awaddr;
    // ...
endinterface
```

## 33.10 Parameterized UVM Components

UVM agents, drivers, monitors, and scoreboards should be parameterized to match the DUT:

```systemverilog
class axi_driver #(int DATA_WIDTH = 32, int ADDR_WIDTH = 32)
    extends uvm_driver #(axi_txn #(DATA_WIDTH, ADDR_WIDTH));
    `uvm_component_param_utils(axi_driver #(DATA_WIDTH, ADDR_WIDTH))
```

Parameterized UVM components scale with the DUT without requiring separate implementations per configuration.

## 33.11 Configuration Management

Manage parameter configurations systematically:

```yaml
Configuration: axi_32b_256d
  DATA_WIDTH: 32
  ADDR_WIDTH: 32
  FIFO_DEPTH: 256
  USE_ECC:    1

Configuration: axi_64b_512d
  DATA_WIDTH: 64
  ADDR_WIDTH: 40
  FIFO_DEPTH: 512
  USE_ECC:    1
```

Define configurations explicitly and track which have been verified.

## 33.12 Verification Strategy for Parameterized Designs

```text
Identify All Parameters → Define Legal Ranges → Define Critical Configurations →
Verify Minimum Configuration → Verify Maximum Configuration →
Verify Default Configuration → Verify Edge Cases →
Automate Multi-Configuration Regression
```

## 33.13 Critical Configurations

Always verify: minimum legal values, maximum legal values, default values, power-of-two boundaries (for depth and width parameters), non-power-of-two values where supported, and configurations that activate generate conditionals.

## 33.14 Configuration Coverage

```systemverilog
covergroup param_cg;
    cp_data_width: coverpoint DATA_WIDTH {
        bins narrow  = {8, 16};
        bins standard = {32, 64};
        bins wide    = {128, 256, 512};
    }
    cp_fifo_depth: coverpoint FIFO_DEPTH {
        bins small  = {[4:15]};
        bins medium = {[16:255]};
        bins large  = {[256:1024]};
    }
endgroup
```

## 33.15 Automated Multi-Configuration Regression

Script regression across configurations:

```python
CONFIGS = [
    {"DATA_WIDTH": 32,  "FIFO_DEPTH": 256, "USE_ECC": 1},
    {"DATA_WIDTH": 64,  "FIFO_DEPTH": 512, "USE_ECC": 1},
    {"DATA_WIDTH": 128, "FIFO_DEPTH": 128, "USE_ECC": 0},
]
for cfg in CONFIGS:
    run_regression(cfg)
```

Automation ensures all critical configurations are covered without manual intervention.

## 33.16 Generate Block Naming

Name generate blocks explicitly for readable hierarchy and simpler debug:

```systemverilog
for (genvar i = 0; i < NUM_CH; i++) begin : gen_ch
    // hierarchy: u_top.gen_ch[2].u_axi_agent
end
```

Unnamed generate blocks produce tool-dependent hierarchy names that complicate waveform analysis.

## 33.17 Common Parameterization Bugs

Incorrect `$clog2` at boundary values, missing parameter validation, hard-coded width inside a parameterized module, generate conditional selecting the wrong branch, localparam calculation error, off-by-one in pointer width, parameter propagation error across hierarchy.

## 33.18 Debug Methodology

```text
Unexpected Behavior → Check Parameter Values → Check Localparam Calculations →
Check $clog2 Results → Check Generate Branch Taken →
Check Generated Hierarchy → Root Cause
```

Always print and verify elaboration-time parameter values before debugging simulation behavior.

## 33.19 Best Practices

Always validate parameters with `$fatal`; use `$clog2` for derived widths; name all generate blocks explicitly; avoid hard-coded constants in parameterized modules; verify minimum, maximum, and boundary configurations; automate multi-configuration regression; parameterize UVM components to match the DUT; document legal parameter ranges.

## 33.20 Chapter Summary

Parameterized RTL and generate constructs are fundamental to professional digital design. Verification engineers must understand parameterization philosophy, generate syntax, parameter validation, configuration management, and the systematic strategy required to demonstrate correctness across all meaningful parameter combinations — not only the default configuration.

## Engineering Exercise

For a parameterized AXI4 data-width converter (DATA_WIDTH: 32/64/128, ADDR_WIDTH: 32/40): (1) identify all parameters; (2) define legal ranges; (3) write `$fatal` parameter validation; (4) create a generate conditional for optional ECC; (5) design a configuration matrix; (6) write a Python regression script; (7) create configuration covergroups; (8) verify minimum and maximum configurations; (9) test `$clog2` boundary values; (10) produce a multi-configuration signoff report.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**Never verify only the default parameter configuration. The most dangerous bugs in parameterized RTL hide at the boundaries — the minimum legal width, the maximum depth, the non-power-of-two case, and the configuration that activates a generate branch no one thought to test.**

# Chapter 34 — Synthesizable RTL Coding Patterns

*The Professional Library of Reusable, Synthesis-Clean Hardware Patterns*

> "RTL patterns are the vocabulary of hardware engineering. Master them, and you can read and verify any digital design."

## Chapter Objective

Professional RTL design reuses proven patterns. This chapter covers the essential synthesizable RTL patterns that verification engineers encounter in every design — ready/valid handshakes, credit-based flow control, arbitration, datapath, control, error handling, and synthesis implications.

## 34.1 Why Patterns Matter

Patterns encode proven engineering solutions. Recognizing a pattern in RTL immediately suggests its verification strategy, common failure modes, and applicable assertions.

## 34.2 Ready/Valid Handshake

The fundamental AXI transfer protocol — the source drives `valid`, the destination drives `ready`, and a transfer occurs when both are asserted simultaneously:

```systemverilog
// Transfer occurs when valid AND ready are both asserted
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        data_reg <= '0;
        data_valid <= 1'b0;
    end else if (valid_in && ready_out) begin
        data_reg   <= data_in;
        data_valid <= 1'b1;
    end else if (ready_out) begin
        data_valid <= 1'b0;
    end
end
```

Verification: `valid` without `ready` (stall), `ready` without `valid` (no transfer), simultaneous assertion (transfer), back-to-back transfers.

## 34.3 Credit-Based Flow Control

Downstream grants credits to upstream; upstream consumes one credit per transaction and waits if none remain:

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        credit_cnt <= INIT_CREDITS;
    else
        credit_cnt <= credit_cnt
                    - (send && credit_cnt > 0)  // consume
                    + return_credit;             // replenish
end
assign can_send = (credit_cnt > 0);
```

Verification: credit exhaustion, credit return, simultaneous consume/return, reset recovery, credit leak detection.

## 34.4 Fixed-Priority Arbiter

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
    grant = '0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) begin
        if (request[i] && grant == '0)
            grant[i] = 1'b1;
    end
end
```

Verification: single requester, multiple simultaneous requesters, priority order, no grant without request, single grant per cycle.

## 34.5 Round-Robin Arbiter

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)
        last_grant <= '0;
    else if (|grant)
        last_grant <= grant;
end

// Rotation: check from last_grant+1 onward, then wrap
always_comb begin
    grant = '0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) begin
        int idx = (last_grant_idx + 1 + i) % N;
        if (request[idx] && grant == '0)
            grant[idx] = 1'b1;
    end
end
```

Verification: rotation order, pointer wrap, priority after starvation, reset state, simultaneous requests.

## 34.6 Synchronous FIFO

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        wr_ptr <= '0;
        rd_ptr <= '0;
        count  <= '0;
    end else begin
        if (wr_en && !full)  begin mem[wr_ptr] <= wdata; wr_ptr <= wr_ptr + 1; count <= count + 1; end
        if (rd_en && !empty) begin rdata <= mem[rd_ptr]; rd_ptr <= rd_ptr + 1; count <= count - 1; end
    end
end
assign full  = (count == DEPTH);
assign empty = (count == 0);
```

Verification: single write, single read, full, empty, simultaneous read/write, overflow protection, underflow protection.

## 34.7 Pipeline Register

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        stage_data  <= '0;
        stage_valid <= 1'b0;
    end else if (pipe_en) begin
        stage_data  <= prev_data;
        stage_valid <= prev_valid;
    end
end
```

Verification: valid propagation, stall behavior (pipe_en deasserted), flush, reset mid-operation.

## 34.8 One-Hot FSM

```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [3:0] {
    ST_IDLE     = 4'b0001,
    ST_REQ      = 4'b0010,
    ST_TRANSFER = 4'b0100,
    ST_DONE     = 4'b1000
} state_t;

state_t state, next;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) state <= ST_IDLE;
    else        state <= next;

always_comb begin
    next = state;
    unique case (state)
        ST_IDLE:     if (req)      next = ST_REQ;
        ST_REQ:      if (grant)    next = ST_TRANSFER;
        ST_TRANSFER: if (done)     next = ST_DONE;
        ST_DONE:                   next = ST_IDLE;
        default:                   next = ST_IDLE;
    endcase
end
```

Verification: every transition, `default` branch (illegal state recovery), reset, simultaneous inputs.

## 34.9 Clock Gating

```systemverilog
// Integrated Clock Gate (ICG)
always_latch begin
    if (!clk) gated_en <= enable;
end
assign gated_clk = clk & gated_en;
```

Verification: enable/disable behavior, glitch-free gating, reset interaction, wake-up latency.

## 34.10 Synchronous Reset Register

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (!rst_n) q <= RESET_VAL;
    else        q <= d;
end
```

Verification: reset value, reset assertion timing, reset release recovery, back-to-back resets.

## 34.11 Asynchronous Reset Register

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) q <= RESET_VAL;
    else        q <= d;
end
```

Verification: async assert (independent of clock), synchronous deassert (with synchronizer), reset value, metastability on release.

## 34.12 Parameterized Shift Register

```systemverilog
module shift_reg #(parameter WIDTH = 8, parameter DEPTH = 4) (
    input  logic             clk, rst_n, en,
    input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] d,
    output logic [WIDTH-1:0] q
);
    logic [WIDTH-1:0] sr [0:DEPTH-1];
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n) foreach (sr[i]) sr[i] <= '0;
        else if (en) begin
            sr[0] <= d;
            for (int i = 1; i < DEPTH; i++) sr[i] <= sr[i-1];
        end
    end
    assign q = sr[DEPTH-1];
endgroup
```

Verification: shift enable, reset, depth boundary, WIDTH boundary.

## 34.13 Gray Counter

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        bin_cnt  <= '0;
        gray_cnt <= '0;
    end else begin
        bin_cnt  <= bin_cnt + 1;
        gray_cnt <= (bin_cnt + 1) ^ ((bin_cnt + 1) >> 1);
    end
end
```

Verification: one-bit change per cycle, wrap-around, reset, and Gray-to-binary conversion correctness.

## 34.14 AXI Write Channel Skeleton

```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [1:0] {
    AW_IDLE = 2'b00,
    AW_ADDR = 2'b01,
    AW_DATA = 2'b10,
    AW_RESP = 2'b11
} aw_state_t;

aw_state_t aw_state, aw_next;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) aw_state <= AW_IDLE;
    else        aw_state <= aw_next;

always_comb begin
    aw_next   = aw_state;
    awready   = 1'b0;
    wready    = 1'b0;
    bvalid    = 1'b0;
    unique case (aw_state)
        AW_IDLE: if (awvalid)           aw_next = AW_ADDR;
        AW_ADDR: begin awready = 1'b1;  aw_next = AW_DATA; end
        AW_DATA: begin wready  = 1'b1;
                       if (wvalid && wlast) aw_next = AW_RESP; end
        AW_RESP: begin bvalid  = 1'b1;
                       if (bready)     aw_next = AW_IDLE; end
    endcase
end
```

Verification: normal write, backpressure on AW, backpressure on W, backpressure on B, reset mid-burst.

## 34.15 Error Detection & Reporting

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        err_valid <= 1'b0;
        err_code  <= '0;
    end else if (parity_error) begin
        err_valid <= 1'b1;
        err_code  <= ERR_PARITY;
    end else if (timeout_error) begin
        err_valid <= 1'b1;
        err_code  <= ERR_TIMEOUT;
    end else if (err_valid && err_clear) begin
        err_valid <= 1'b0;
        err_code  <= '0;
    end
end
```

Verification: each error type, simultaneous errors, error clear, recovery, overflow when unclaimed.

## 34.16 Synthesis Implications

Common RTL constructs and their synthesis behavior:

| Construct | Synthesis Result |
|---|---|
| `always_ff` | Flip-flops |
| `always_comb` | Combinational logic |
| `always_latch` | Latch (use carefully) |
| `unique case` | Priority-free decoder |
| `priority case` | Priority decoder |
| `if-else chain` | Priority decoder |
| Incomplete `case` | Latch (avoid) |
| Missing `default` | Potential latch |

## 34.17 Common Synthesis Pitfalls

Incomplete sensitivity list (pre-SV), incomplete case statement, latch inference, multiple drivers, combinational feedback loop, synthesis-simulation mismatch from blocking/non-blocking confusion, parameter-dependent width truncation.

## 34.18 Verification Strategy

For each pattern: verify normal operation, all boundary conditions, error injection, reset behavior, interaction with other patterns, and synthesis-simulation equivalence for critical paths.

## 34.19 Chapter Summary

RTL patterns are the fundamental vocabulary of digital design. Professional verification engineers should recognize each pattern, understand its implementation, know its verification requirements, and be prepared to write assertions and coverage for it. Pattern recognition dramatically accelerates both verification planning and debugging.

## Engineering Exercise

Implement and verify a parameterized AXI4-Lite slave register block: (1) use a ready/valid handshake; (2) implement an FSM with a `default` branch; (3) add error detection and reporting; (4) parameterize data and address widths; (5) write directed tests for every pattern; (6) write assertions for handshake correctness, FSM legality, and error reporting; (7) build functional coverage for each pattern; (8) inject synthesis-simulation mismatch by testing blocking/non-blocking behavior; (9) automate regression for two configurations; (10) produce a verification report.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**Every RTL pattern has a known verification strategy. When you recognize the pattern, you already know the assertions, the corner cases, the coverage model, and the most likely failure modes — before reading a single line of the implementation.**

# Chapter 35 — Common RTL Bugs & Failure Modes

*The Complete Catalog of Recurring Hardware Defects*

> "Every silicon escape is a lesson. This chapter is the collection of those lessons, before they cost you."

## Chapter Objective

RTL bugs follow recognizable patterns. Understanding the most common defect classes — their root causes, symptoms, detection methods, and prevention strategies — makes verification engineers dramatically more effective. This chapter catalogs the recurring RTL failure modes across reset, clocking, FSM, arithmetic, memory, protocol, power, and synthesis.

## 35.1 Why Bug Catalogs Matter

Experienced engineers recognize failure patterns quickly because they have seen them before. This chapter accelerates that pattern recognition by presenting a structured catalog of the most common RTL defects in production silicon design.

## 35.2 Bug Classification

```text
Reset Bugs → Clocking Bugs → FSM Bugs → Arithmetic Bugs → Memory Bugs →
Protocol Bugs → CDC/RDC Bugs → Power Bugs → Synthesis Bugs → Integration Bugs
```

Each class has distinct symptoms, detection methods, and prevention strategies.

## 35.3 Reset Bugs

**Missing Reset:** register lacks a reset condition — indeterminate initial state, X-propagation, simulation-silicon mismatch.
**Wrong Reset Value:** register initializes to an incorrect value — immediate functional failure.
**Incomplete Reset:** some registers in a module reset while others do not — partial initialization failure.
**Async Reset Without Synchronizer:** reset deasserts without synchronization — metastability on recovery.
**Reset Race Condition:** logic samples data during the reset window — X-capture or incorrect initialization.

Detection: assertions on initial values, lint, reset-value checkers. Prevention: reset all registers; use async-assert/synchronous-deassert; verify reset values at elaboration.

## 35.4 Clocking Bugs

**Missing Clock Enable:** register always captures rather than capturing only when enabled — incorrect data.
**Clock Enable Race:** enable sampled on incorrect clock edge — timing-dependent failure.
**Gated Clock Glitch:** combinational logic on the clock path — spurious clock edges.
**Incorrect Clock Division:** wrong ratio generates incorrect derived frequency.
**Clock Mux Glitch:** switching clock source without glitch-free mux — spurious edges.

Detection: lint, CDC analysis, STA. Prevention: use ICG cells; avoid combinational clock logic; verify clock mux behavior.

## 35.5 FSM Bugs

**Missing Default:** incomplete case without default — latch inference or X-state.
**Illegal State Lock-Up:** no recovery from an illegal state — FSM hangs permanently.
**Wrong Transition Condition:** incorrect Boolean expression routes traffic to the wrong state.
**Off-by-One Cycle:** action taken one cycle too early or too late.
**Missing Self-Loop:** FSM does not remain in a waiting state when expected.
**Unreachable State:** a state exists in RTL but can never be entered — dead code.

Detection: FSM coverage, state assertions, formal reachability. Prevention: always include a default branch; verify every transition; add illegal-state recovery; use formal to prove deadlock freedom.

## 35.6 Arithmetic Bugs

**Integer Overflow:** result exceeds bit width — silent wrap-around corruption.
**Signed/Unsigned Confusion:** incorrect interpretation of two's-complement values.
**Division by Zero:** undefined result — simulation X, silicon implementation-specific.
**Shift Amount Overflow:** shift by more than the operand width.
**Carry/Borrow Error:** missing carry propagation in multi-word arithmetic.
**Accumulator Saturation Missing:** accumulator overflows without saturation protection.

Detection: arithmetic assertions (`overflow`, `saturation`), directed boundary tests. Prevention: size operands carefully; add overflow detection; validate signed/unsigned semantics; test maximum values.

## 35.7 Width & Type Bugs

**Width Mismatch:** implicit truncation or zero-extension produces incorrect values.
**Signed/Unsigned Port Mismatch:** signed value connected to unsigned port — sign extension lost.
**Parameter Width Error:** `$clog2` result used without validating boundary behavior.
**Implicit Wire Width:** undriven bits default to Z — incorrect downstream behavior.

Detection: lint (width checks), waveform inspection. Prevention: explicitly declare all widths; use lint to enforce width matching; validate `$clog2` at boundaries.

## 35.8 Latch Bugs

**Unintended Latch:** incomplete `if-else` or `case` in `always_comb` — latch inferred.
**Glitchy Latch Enable:** combinational logic on latch enable — spurious sampling.
**Latch Timing Violation:** latch transparent window too narrow — data not captured.

Detection: lint (latch detection), synthesis warnings. Prevention: use `always_ff` for sequential; always include a default assignment in `always_comb`; avoid latches unless intentional.

## 35.9 Combinational Loop Bugs

**Feedback Loop:** output depends on itself without a register — oscillation or X-propagation.
**Indirect Loop:** A → B → C → A through multiple modules — difficult to detect manually.

Detection: lint (loop detection), synthesis warnings, X-propagation analysis. Prevention: never create combinational feedback; review all `always_comb` output dependencies.

## 35.10 CDC Bugs

**Unsynchronized Crossing:** signal used directly across clock domains — metastability.
**Multi-Bit Bus Without Coordination:** each bit synchronized independently — illegal intermediate value.
**Pulse Too Short:** pulse width less than one destination clock period — pulse may be lost.
**Reconvergence:** diverged paths from one source recombine — glitch in destination.
**Synchronizer Bypass:** combinational logic after the synchronizer — metastability propagation.

Detection: CDC analysis tools, assertions. Prevention: synchronize every crossing; use handshakes or async FIFOs for multi-bit; verify pulse width.

## 35.11 RDC Bugs

**Missing Isolation:** powered-down domain drives active domain — X-propagation.
**Wrong Isolation Value:** incorrect driven value corrupts downstream protocol.
**Incorrect Reset Sequencing:** reset deassertion before isolation is released.
**Missing Reset Synchronizer:** reset crosses domain without synchronization.

Detection: RDC analysis tools, isolation assertions. Prevention: isolate before power-down; synchronize reset deassert; verify every crossing.

## 35.12 Memory Bugs

**Address Aliasing:** multiple addresses map to the same location — read-after-write corruption.
**Off-by-One Address:** boundary condition omits the first or last address.
**ECC Miscalculation:** incorrect syndrome — undetected errors or false corrections.
**Initialization Missing:** memory read before write — indeterminate or X value.
**Simultaneous Conflicting Access:** two ports write to the same address — undefined result.

Detection: boundary-address tests, ECC syndrome injection, read-before-write detection. Prevention: verify all boundary addresses; test ECC; initialize memories before use.

## 35.13 Protocol Bugs

**Missing Handshake:** transaction committed without both sides asserting.
**Ordering Violation:** response received out of order — AXI ID violation.
**Credit Leak:** credits consumed but never returned — credit exhaustion over time.
**Timeout Handling Missing:** blocked transaction never recovers — system hang.
**Outstanding Transaction Limit Exceeded:** more outstanding than the protocol allows.

Detection: protocol assertions, scoreboard, credit counter monitor. Prevention: implement timeouts; verify outstanding-transaction limits; monitor credits with assertions.

## 35.14 Power Management Bugs

**Missing Isolation:** undefined values propagate during power-down.
**Incorrect Retention:** state not preserved or incorrectly restored.
**Power Sequence Error:** power removed before isolation is complete.
**Wakeup Hang:** power-up sequence does not complete — system remains unresponsive.

Detection: power-aware simulation, power assertions. Prevention: verify every power-state transition; use UPF/CPF-aware simulation; sequence formally.

## 35.15 Synthesis-Simulation Mismatch Bugs

**Blocking vs. Non-Blocking Confusion:** RTL uses blocking assignment in a sequential block — simulation correct, synthesis differs.
**Initial Block Ignored:** `initial` block initializes simulation but is not synthesized.
**Timing-Dependent Behavior:** simulation result depends on evaluation order — undefined in synthesis.
**Unsupported Construct:** a simulation construct not synthesized — behavior diverges post-synthesis.

Detection: lint, gate-level simulation, formal equivalence checking. Prevention: use `always_ff` for sequential; avoid `initial` blocks in synthesizable RTL; simulate the gate-level netlist.

## 35.16 Integration Bugs

**Interface Mismatch:** signal width, direction, or timing differs between connected modules.
**Protocol Version Mismatch:** AXI3 connected to AXI4 without a bridge.
**Address Map Conflict:** two peripherals respond to the same address.
**Clock/Reset Mismatch:** different subsystems assume different clock or reset relationships.
**Missing Tie-Off:** unused inputs left floating — indeterminate behavior.

Detection: connectivity checks, protocol assertions, integration tests. Prevention: review all interfaces before integration; use interface wrappers; validate the address map.

## 35.17 Bug Prevention Summary

| Bug Class | Primary Prevention |
|---|---|
| Reset | Reset all registers; lint; async-assert/sync-deassert |
| Clocking | ICG cells; no combinational clock logic; lint |
| FSM | Default branch; formal reachability; transition assertions |
| Arithmetic | Size operands; overflow assertions; boundary tests |
| Width/Type | Explicit widths; lint width checks; `$clog2` validation |
| Latch | `always_ff`; complete case; lint latch detection |
| Combinational Loop | Lint; no combinational feedback |
| CDC | Synchronizers; CDC analysis; async FIFO for multi-bit |
| RDC | Isolation; RDC analysis; reset synchronizers |
| Memory | Boundary tests; ECC injection; initialization checks |
| Protocol | Assertions; scoreboards; outstanding-transaction limits |
| Power | UPF/CPF simulation; power sequencing formal proof |
| Synth-Sim | Gate-level simulation; formal equivalence |
| Integration | Interface reviews; address-map validation |

## 35.18 Chapter Summary

RTL bugs follow predictable patterns. Professional verification engineers recognize defect classes, understand their causes, know which techniques detect them, and design verification environments that specifically target known failure modes. A systematic approach to bug classification dramatically improves verification effectiveness and reduces silicon escape rates.

## Engineering Exercise

For a parameterized AXI4 DMA controller: (1) identify the ten highest-risk bug classes; (2) create one directed test per class; (3) write one assertion per class; (4) design a prevention strategy per class; (5) plan a regression targeting each defect class; (6) create a bug classification template; (7) analyze a past project for missed bug classes; (8) estimate residual risk after mitigation; (9) present findings in a design review format; (10) update the project verification plan based on the analysis.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**Every verification plan should explicitly answer: which defect classes are we targeting, how are we targeting each one, and which ones remain as accepted residual risk?**

Verification that does not explicitly plan for known failure modes is incomplete by definition — and the failures it misses will be found in silicon, not simulation.

# Chapter 36 — Design Reviews for Verification Engineers

*Extracting Maximum Value from Every Technical Review*

> "A bug found in a review costs nothing to fix. The same bug found in silicon costs everything."

## Chapter Objective

Design reviews are among the most cost-effective activities in hardware engineering — catching defects before simulation, synthesis, or tapeout dramatically reduces cost and schedule risk. This chapter covers specification reviews, microarchitecture reviews, RTL reviews, verification plan reviews, coverage reviews, and signoff reviews — with structured checklists for each.

## 36.1 Why Reviews Matter

A review defect costs minutes to fix. A simulation defect costs hours. A tapeout defect costs weeks. A silicon defect costs months, money, and customer trust. Investing in thorough reviews always reduces total project cost.

## 36.2 Review Principles

Reviews should be: objective (evaluate the work, not the person), evidence-based (reference specifications and standards), constructive (improve, not criticize), timely (early in the phase), documented (action items recorded), and followed-up (items closed).

## 36.3 Roles in a Review

**Author:** presents the work, answers questions, owns action items. **Reviewer:** identifies issues, asks clarifying questions, suggests improvements. **Moderator:** keeps focus, manages time, records decisions. **Observer:** optional learner who does not drive discussion.

## 36.4 Specification Reviews

Objectives: identify ambiguity, contradictions, missing requirements, incorrect assumptions, missing error handling, undefined timing, and security gaps.

Checklist:
- Is every feature described completely and unambiguously?
- Are all timing relationships defined?
- Is reset behavior specified?
- Is error handling defined for every error type?
- Are performance targets measurable?
- Are security assumptions explicitly stated?
- Is every interface fully specified?
- Are all parameters and their legal ranges defined?
- Is the behavior defined for illegal inputs?
- Are out-of-scope items explicitly listed?

## 36.5 Microarchitecture Reviews

Objectives: validate architectural decisions, identify integration risks, review clock/reset strategy, evaluate performance.

Checklist:
- Does the microarchitecture satisfy every specification requirement?
- Are all clock domains identified and documented?
- Are all reset domains identified and sequenced?
- Is the power architecture defined?
- Are all CDC crossings identified with synchronization methods?
- Is the memory map complete and non-overlapping?
- Are all interfaces compatible with adjacent blocks?
- Are performance targets achievable given the chosen architecture?
- Are known high-risk areas flagged for deeper verification?
- Is the microarchitecture document up to date?

## 36.6 RTL Reviews

Objectives: identify bugs before simulation, review coding quality, validate synthesis assumptions.

Checklist:
- Does every register have a reset?
- Are all signals driven by exactly one source?
- Are all `case` statements complete with `default`?
- Are there any unintended latches?
- Are all clock enables correct?
- Are parameterizations validated with `$fatal`?
- Is the FSM complete — including illegal-state recovery?
- Is the CDC strategy implemented as documented?
- Is the reset synchronizer present where required?
- Does the module match the microarchitecture specification?

## 36.7 Verification Plan Reviews

Objectives: validate coverage strategy, confirm risk alignment, review signoff criteria.

Checklist:
- Are all specification requirements traced to verification items?
- Is the risk matrix complete and accurate?
- Is the coverage plan specific and measurable?
- Are assertions planned for all critical behaviors?
- Is the regression strategy defined?
- Are edge cases and error scenarios included?
- Is the testbench architecture documented?
- Are signoff criteria defined and measurable?
- Are reuse opportunities identified?
- Is the schedule realistic given the scope?

## 36.8 Testbench Architecture Reviews

Objectives: evaluate reusability, scalability, and correctness of the verification environment.

Checklist:
- Is the environment structured following UVM hierarchy?
- Are all interfaces parameterized?
- Is the scoreboard independent of protocol implementation details?
- Are assertions integrated throughout the environment?
- Is the reference model separated from the DUT-specific logic?
- Is the configuration database usage consistent?
- Are all agents reusable across multiple testbenches?
- Is the coverage model aligned with the verification plan?
- Is factory override possible for all major components?
- Is the environment documented sufficiently for team use?

## 36.9 Coverage Reviews

Objectives: confirm coverage models are meaningful, identify gaps, evaluate closure progress.

Checklist:
- Does every covergroup reflect specification requirements rather than RTL structure?
- Are bins meaningful and mutually exclusive?
- Are illegal bins correctly excluded?
- Does cross coverage capture important feature interactions?
- Are coverage holes classified with root-cause analysis?
- Is waiver justification sufficient and approved?
- Does code coverage supplement functional coverage without replacing it?
- Are assertion coverage metrics reviewed?
- Is requirement coverage tracked separately?
- Is the overall coverage picture consistent with signoff readiness?

## 36.10 Regression Reviews

Objectives: assess regression health, identify systematic failures, evaluate stability.

Checklist:
- Is the pass rate trending upward?
- Are failures grouped by root cause rather than reviewed individually?
- Are flaky tests identified and root-caused?
- Is regression runtime acceptable?
- Are all critical scenarios included?
- Is the regression infrastructure stable?
- Are failures from recent RTL changes identified?
- Is the regression being run at appropriate frequency?

## 36.11 Signoff Reviews

Objectives: confirm tapeout readiness based on objective evidence.

Checklist:
- Are all requirements traced and verified?
- Is functional coverage at goal with remaining holes documented?
- Is code coverage reviewed and accepted?
- Are assertions passing with vacuous-pass analysis complete?
- Is regression stable over multiple runs?
- Are all critical bugs resolved or waived with documented justification?
- Is performance verified at architectural targets?
- Is power verified including all power states?
- Is security verified?
- Is the documentation complete and accurate?

## 36.12 Conducting Effective Reviews

Preparation is 80% of a good review: distribute materials in advance, prepare specific questions, use checklists, focus on intent as well as implementation, separate question-raising from problem-solving (solve offline), record all findings with owners and due dates.

## 36.13 Common Review Mistakes

Reading code aloud without analyzing intent; focusing on style rather than correctness; skipping preparation; failing to record action items; not following up on closure; allowing reviews to become blame sessions; reviewing too much material in one session (two hours maximum).

## 36.14 Review Documentation

Every review produces: review ID, date, participants, material reviewed, findings list (severity/description/owner/due date), decisions made, and review outcome (approved/approved-with-actions/needs-revision).

## 36.15 Severity Classification

| Severity | Description | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Functional error or silicon risk | Must fix before proceeding |
| Major | Significant issue affecting quality | Must fix before signoff |
| Minor | Style or maintainability issue | Fix at author's discretion |
| Question | Clarification needed | Respond and document |
| Suggestion | Optional improvement | Optional |

## 36.16 Chapter Summary

Design reviews are the highest-leverage quality activity in hardware engineering. Professional verification engineers contribute to every review type — specification, microarchitecture, RTL, verification plan, testbench, coverage, regression, and signoff — using structured checklists, objective evaluation, and disciplined follow-up to maximize defect detection before silicon.

## Engineering Exercise

Conduct a mock review of a simple AXI4-Lite slave: (1) review the specification for ambiguity; (2) review the microarchitecture for CDC and reset risks; (3) review the RTL for latch, reset, and FSM correctness; (4) review the verification plan for requirement traceability; (5) review the testbench architecture for reusability; (6) review the coverage model for specification alignment; (7) classify all findings by severity; (8) assign owners and due dates; (9) write a review report; (10) define closure criteria.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**A review is not a performance — it is a structured search for risk. Prepare thoroughly, ask hard questions, record everything, and follow up relentlessly. The goal is not to find the most issues in the room; it is to ensure none of them reach silicon.**

**Next — Chapter 37: RTL Debugging for Verification Engineers.** Advanced RTL debugging: waveform analysis, X-propagation, delta cycles, simulation semantics, log file analysis, protocol-level debugging, assertion-guided analysis, systematic root cause techniques, and professional debug workflow.

# Chapter 37 — RTL Debugging for Verification Engineers

*Advanced Techniques for Systematic Hardware Debug*

> "Amateur debuggers look at signals. Professional debuggers look at behavior. Expert debuggers look at intent."

## Chapter Objective

RTL debugging is a core professional skill. This chapter covers waveform analysis, X-propagation, delta cycles, simulation semantics, log file analysis, protocol-level debugging, assertion-guided debug, systematic root-cause techniques, vendor tool techniques (VCS, Xcelium, Questa), and the professional debug workflow.

## 37.1 The Debug Mindset

Debug is not random exploration — it is **hypothesis-driven scientific method**: observe the symptom → form a hypothesis → design an experiment → interpret results → revise the hypothesis → repeat until root cause is identified.

## 37.2 The Debug Pyramid

```text
Observed Failure
      ↓
Understand the Specification Intent
      ↓
Identify the Architectural Level of the Failure
      ↓
Isolate to a Module or Block
      ↓
Locate the Signal or FSM State
      ↓
Identify the Root Cause
      ↓
Fix → Verify → Regression
```

Always begin at the top, never the bottom.

## 37.3 Simulation Semantics Engineers Must Know

**Delta cycles:** within a single simulation timestep, multiple evaluation passes occur before time advances. Non-blocking assignments (`<=`) schedule updates for the next delta; blocking assignments (`=`) take effect immediately. Race conditions between `always` blocks in the same timestep produce non-deterministic behavior.

**Zero-time loops:** if combinational logic oscillates without advancing time, the simulator detects a zero-time loop and halts with an error.

**Event-driven simulation:** only signals that change drive re-evaluation. Missed sensitivity-list entries produce incorrect simulation results.

**X-state semantics:** `X` propagates through logic. A three-input AND gate with one `X` input produces `X` output when the other inputs are 1, but correctly produces 0 if either non-X input is 0.

## 37.4 Waveform Analysis Methodology

Read waveforms like a protocol specification, not like a list of signals:

```text
1. Identify the transaction boundaries (request/response)
2. Verify handshake protocol (valid/ready timing)
3. Locate the first divergence from expected behavior
4. Trace backward from the divergence to the root cause
5. Never fix a symptom — find the cause
```

## 37.5 X-Propagation Debug

X in a signal indicates one of: uninitialized register, multiple drivers, unresolved metastability, or deliberate simulation semantics. Methodology:

```text
X observed → Identify source → Was this register reset? → Check reset logic →
Check multiple drivers → Check CDC path → Check initial block
```

Common mistake: disabling X-propagation globally. Instead, investigate each X — every one represents a real engineering concern.

## 37.6 Delta Cycle Debug

When two signals appear to change simultaneously in a waveform but the behavior is incorrect:

```text
1. Check whether both use blocking vs. non-blocking assignment
2. Identify whether they share an always block
3. Look for combinational dependency between them
4. Use $display at specific timesteps to observe delta-cycle behavior
```

## 37.7 Log File Analysis

Simulation logs contain: UVM phase transitions, factory registrations, `uvm_fatal`/`uvm_error`/`uvm_warning` messages, assertion failures, scoreboard mismatches, and `$display` output.

Professional log analysis:
```text
1. Search for FATAL and ERROR first
2. Identify the earliest failure timestamp
3. Correlate the log timestamp with waveform time
4. Trace the failure backward through UVM messages
5. Never analyze only the last error — find the first
```

## 37.8 Protocol-Level Debug

For AXI, APB, CHI, PCIe, USB — debug the **protocol transaction** before the **signal implementation**:

```text
AXI Write Debug:
1. Is AWVALID asserted? Is AWREADY returned?
2. Is WVALID asserted with correct data and strobe?
3. Is WLAST asserted on the final beat?
4. Is BRESP returning the correct response code?
5. Are outstanding IDs being tracked correctly?
```

A protocol-level scoreboard that compares request-response pairs is more powerful than signal-by-signal waveform inspection.

## 37.9 Assertion-Guided Debug

When an assertion fires, it provides:
- Precise simulation time
- The specific property that was violated
- The signals involved

Use assertions as debug accelerators:
```systemverilog
// Instead of searching for a handshake violation:
property axi_valid_stable;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (awvalid && !awready) |=> awvalid;
endproperty
assert_awvalid_stable: assert property (axi_valid_stable)
    else $error("AWVALID dropped before AWREADY — AXI protocol violation at time %0t", $time);
```

## 37.10 Scoreboard Debug

When a scoreboard mismatch fires:
```text
1. Print the expected transaction in full
2. Print the observed transaction in full
3. Identify which field mismatches
4. Trace the expected value back to the stimulus
5. Trace the observed value back through the DUT
6. Verify the reference model is correct before fixing the DUT
```

A scoreboard bug masquerading as a DUT bug is extremely common.

## 37.11 UVM Phase Debug

When a simulation hangs or phases do not complete:
```text
1. Enable UVM phase debugging: +UVM_PHASE_TRACE
2. Identify the blocking phase
3. Check for objections raised but never dropped
4. Check for sequences that never finish
5. Check for back-to-back timeouts
```

## 37.12 Seed Reproducibility

Every constrained-random failure must be reproducible:
```text
Failed seed: +ntb_random_seed=<seed> (VCS)
             +UVM_TESTNAME=<test> +UVM_SEED=<seed> (Questa/Xcelium)
```

Lock the seed, reproduce the failure, minimize the stimulus, then debug. Never debug a non-reproducible failure — fix reproducibility first.

## 37.13 Simulator-Specific Techniques

**VCS:**
```
+vcs+dumpvars+<file>.vpd   — dump waveforms
-debug_access+all          — enable full debug access
+define+SIMULATION         — pass simulation defines
```

**Xcelium:**
```
-access +rwc               — full read/write/callback access
-database -shm <file>      — SHM waveform database
-uvm_verbosity UVM_HIGH    — maximum UVM verbosity
```

**Questa:**
```
vlog -sv -work <lib>       — compile SystemVerilog
vsim -voptargs=+acc        — enable full visibility
log -r /*                  — log all signals recursively
```

## 37.14 Reducing a Failing Test

Once a failure is reproduced, minimize it:
```text
1. Remove unrelated stimulus
2. Reduce burst length to minimum that still fails
3. Remove unrelated UVM components
4. Replace CRV with directed replay of the failing scenario
5. Create the smallest possible directed test that reproduces the bug
```

A minimal reproduction dramatically accelerates root cause analysis and provides a regression test.

## 37.15 Common Debug Anti-Patterns

**Random RTL editing:** modifying RTL without understanding the cause — shifts the failure, never fixes it. **Waveform fishing:** scrolling through waveforms without a specific hypothesis — wastes time. **Blaming the tool:** simulator bugs exist but are rare — exhausting RTL and testbench explanations first is always correct. **Disabling assertions:** removing the detection mechanism to avoid investigating the symptom. **Fixing the wrong level:** patching a protocol violation at the signal level when the root cause is architectural.

## 37.16 Root Cause Classification

After finding the root cause, classify it from Chapter 35's taxonomy. This closes the debugging loop by connecting findings to prevention — enabling the verification plan and assertion library to be updated so the same class of bug is detected earlier in future projects.

## 37.17 Debug Documentation

Every significant debug session produces:
```yaml
Bug ID:
Summary:
Environment: RTL revision, seed, simulator version, compile options
Reproduction: exact command to reproduce
Root Cause: one sentence
Fix: what changed and why
Regression: which test confirms the fix
Lessons Learned: how to detect this class earlier
Prevention: assertion or coverage added
```

## 37.18 Chapter Summary

RTL debugging is a systematic, hypothesis-driven discipline. Professional verification engineers understand simulation semantics (delta cycles, X-propagation, event-driven evaluation), analyze failures at the protocol and architectural level before examining signals, use assertions and scoreboards as debug accelerators, apply simulator-specific tools effectively, minimize failures before analyzing them, and document root causes for organizational learning.

## Engineering Exercise

Given a failing AXI4 burst write sequence: (1) reproduce and lock the seed; (2) enable full simulator debug access; (3) identify the first simulation timestamp of the error; (4) correlate the log with the waveform; (5) trace the protocol transaction through AW, W, and B channels; (6) identify which assertion fires; (7) trace backward to root cause; (8) minimize the failing test; (9) fix the RTL or testbench; (10) document the root cause, fix, and prevention measure.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**Debug architecture before RTL. Debug transactions before signals. Debug causes before symptoms. And always ask: which assertion would have caught this earlier — then write it.**

The best debugging session ends not only with a fix, but with a new assertion, a new coverage point, or an improved verification plan that ensures the same failure class never reaches silicon again.

# Chapter 38 — Lint Methodology for Design & Verification Engineers

*Automated Static Analysis as a First Line of Defense*

> "Lint finds the bugs your simulation never exercises and your reviews never see."

## Chapter Objective

Lint is automated static analysis applied to RTL before simulation. It detects coding errors, unintended latches, width mismatches, CDC violations, reset issues, clock problems, and synthesis-simulation mismatches — often in seconds, without requiring a testbench. This chapter covers lint philosophy, common rule categories, tool usage (Spyglass, Ascent Lint, Questa Lint, VC SpyGlass), waiver management, CDC lint, synthesis lint, coding-standard enforcement, and integration into the verification flow.

## 38.1 What is Lint?

Lint applies a set of design rules to RTL source code without simulation. It identifies constructs that are legal SystemVerilog but incorrect, dangerous, non-portable, or non-synthesizable — catching bugs that simulation may never exercise.

## 38.2 Why Lint Matters

Many RTL bugs are never simulated because: the testbench lacks the specific sequence, the coverage model misses the scenario, or the bug is in dead code. Lint finds these bugs statically — before a single simulation run.

## 38.3 Lint vs. Simulation vs. Formal

| Technique | Explores | Speed | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lint | All code paths statically | Seconds to minutes | Minimal |
| Simulation | Exercised paths only | Minutes to hours | Significant |
| Formal | All paths within constraints | Minutes to days | Significant |

Lint, simulation, and formal are complementary — not alternatives.

## 38.4 Lint Rule Categories

**Functional:** latch inference, multiple drivers, incomplete sensitivity, combinational loop, undriven input, X-assignment.
**Synthesis:** non-synthesizable constructs, `initial` block usage, system task usage, unsupported operators.
**Clock/Reset:** gated clock, missing reset, async reset without synchronizer, clock enable polarity.
**CDC:** unsynchronized crossings, multi-bit violations, reconvergence, synchronizer placement.
**Width:** width mismatch, implicit truncation, sign extension, parameter-dependent width.
**Naming/Style:** naming conventions, inconsistent port declarations, module header completeness.
**Portability:** tool-specific constructs, tool-specific pragmas, language version.

## 38.5 Critical Lint Rules

Rules that should never be waived without engineering review:

```text
- Latch inference (unintentional)
- Combinational loop
- Multiple drivers on the same net
- Missing reset
- Unsynchronized CDC crossing
- Width truncation on port connection
- Undriven input port (other than intentional tie-offs)
- Non-synthesizable construct in synthesizable RTL
```

## 38.6 Common Lint Findings

**Latch inference:**
```systemverilog
// Missing else → latch inferred on 'out'
always_comb
    if (sel) out = a;   // 'out' holds when sel=0 — latch
```

**Width mismatch:**
```systemverilog
logic [7:0]  narrow;
logic [15:0] wide;
assign narrow = wide;   // implicit truncation — lint flags this
```

**Unsynchronized CDC:**
```systemverilog
// clk_a domain signal used directly in clk_b domain — lint error
always_ff @(posedge clk_b)
    data_b <= data_a;   // missing synchronizer
```

**Incomplete sensitivity:**
```systemverilog
// Verilog-era bug: b missing from sensitivity list
always @(a)
    out = a & b;   // b change not evaluated — sim/synth mismatch
```

## 38.7 Lint Flow

```text
RTL Source → Lint Tool → Rule Evaluation → Findings Report →
Engineer Review → Fix or Waiver → Clean Lint → Proceed to Simulation
```

Lint should run before simulation, before synthesis, and after every significant RTL change.

## 38.8 Spyglass

Industry-leading lint tool from Synopsys. Key invocation:

```tcl
# Spyglass lint run
read_file -type verilog  {src/rtl/*.sv}
set_option    -top        my_module
set_option    -enable_cdc yes
current_goal  lint/lint_rtl
run_goal
report_results -file lint_report.rpt
```

## 38.9 Questa Lint (Mentor/Siemens)

```tcl
# Questa Lint invocation
vlog -sv -work lint_lib src/rtl/*.sv
vlint -rules all -top my_module -report lint.rpt
```

## 38.10 Ascent Lint (Real Intent)

Particularly strong on CDC and RDC analysis:

```tcl
analyze -sv09 {src/rtl/*.sv}
elaborate -top my_module
verify
report -file lint_report.rpt
```

## 38.11 CDC Lint

CDC-specific lint rules detect:
- Unsynchronized crossings
- Multi-bit bus crossings without coordination
- Pulse-width violations
- Reconvergence paths
- Synchronizer bypass

CDC lint complements CDC simulation — static analysis finds structural violations while simulation validates functional behavior across clock ratios.

## 38.12 RDC Lint

RDC-specific lint rules detect:
- Missing isolation cells
- Incorrect isolation-cell placement
- Reset crossing without synchronizer
- Incorrect reset sequencing

## 38.13 Synthesis Lint

Synthesis lint ensures RTL is synthesis-clean:
- No `initial` blocks in synthesizable code
- No `$display`, `$monitor`, `$finish` in synthesizable code
- No `#delay` constructs
- No `fork`/`join` in synthesizable code
- No non-synthesizable operators

## 38.14 Waiver Management

Not every lint finding represents a real bug. Waivers document intentional exceptions:

```tcl
# Spyglass waiver syntax
waive -rule W240 -regexp ".*tie_high.*" \
      -comment "Intentional tie-off — reviewed by [engineer] on [date]"
```

Waiver requirements: engineering justification, reviewer approval, expiry date, owner, and impact statement. Waivers should be reviewed at every project milestone.

## 38.15 Lint Waivers vs. Fixes

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| True bug | Fix the RTL |
| Intentional pattern (e.g., ICG latch) | Waiver with justification |
| False positive from tool limitation | Waiver with tool version note |
| Deprecated construct that works | Fix to modern equivalent |
| Style violation with no functional impact | Fix or team-policy waiver |

Always prefer fixes over waivers.

## 38.16 Lint Severity Classification

**Error:** must fix before proceeding (functional risk). **Warning:** should fix; investigate if waived. **Info:** advisory; fix if feasible. **Suppressed:** waived with justification. A clean lint run should have zero errors and documented justification for every warning waiver.

## 38.17 Lint in the Verification Flow

```text
RTL Check-in → Automated Lint → Gate on Errors →
Review Warnings → Fix or Waive → Update Waiver Database →
Lint Report in Signoff Package
```

Lint should be a gate, not an afterthought. Blocking simulation on lint errors prevents defects from accumulating.

## 38.18 Coding Standard Enforcement

Lint enforces naming conventions, header format, port declaration style, comment requirements, and module structure. Consistent style reduces review time and improves team velocity.

```systemverilog
// Naming conventions enforced by lint rules
// Signals:       lowercase with underscores (axi_wdata)
// Parameters:    UPPER_CASE (DATA_WIDTH)
// Localparams:   UPPER_CASE (PTR_WIDTH)
// Instances:     u_ prefix (u_fifo, u_axi_master)
// Generate:      gen_ prefix (gen_channels)
// Clocks:        clk_ prefix (clk_cpu, clk_ddr)
// Resets:        rst_n (active-low) or rst (active-high)
// Interfaces:    _if suffix (axi_if, apb_if)
```

## 38.19 Lint Metrics

Track: total findings, errors, warnings, waivers, waiver age, new findings per RTL change, and lint clean milestone dates. Trending metrics reveal RTL quality over time.

## 38.20 Lint Signoff

Lint signoff criteria: zero errors, all warnings reviewed and either fixed or waived with documented justification, waivers reviewed and approved, CDC and RDC lint clean, synthesis lint clean, lint report included in tapeout package.

## 38.21 Common Lint Mistakes

Running lint only once at project end; treating all warnings as noise; accumulating waivers without review; not running CDC lint; skipping lint after major RTL changes; not integrating lint into CI/CD pipelines.

## 38.22 Chapter Summary

Lint is the fastest, lowest-cost defect-detection mechanism available. Professional verification engineers treat lint as a mandatory first step — a gate before simulation — and maintain a clean, waiver-reviewed lint database throughout the project. Lint finds bugs that simulation never exercises, makes RTL reviews more productive, and reduces debugging time.

## Engineering Exercise

For a parameterized AXI4 slave: (1) run Spyglass or equivalent lint; (2) classify all findings by severity and category; (3) fix all latch-inference and width-mismatch findings; (4) run CDC lint and identify all crossings; (5) write justified waivers for intentional ICG latches; (6) enforce naming conventions; (7) run synthesis lint; (8) generate a lint report; (9) define lint signoff criteria; (10) integrate lint into the CI/CD regression pipeline.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**Run lint before simulation, not instead of simulation — and treat a lint error as seriously as a simulation failure. A bug that lint finds in thirty seconds is a bug that simulation might take thirty hours to expose, and silicon might never expose at all.**

**Next — Chapter 39: Design for Test (DFT) Basics for Verification Engineers.** Scan chains, ATPG, MBIST, LBIST, boundary scan, JTAG, DFT insertion, test coverage, DFT verification, and the relationship between design verification and manufacturing test.

# Chapter 39 — Design for Test (DFT) Basics for Verification Engineers

*Understanding Manufacturing Test & Its Relationship to Functional Verification*

> "Functional verification proves the design is correct. DFT proves the manufactured silicon is correct."

## Chapter Objective

DFT (Design for Test) enables efficient manufacturing testing of silicon. While DFT engineering is a specialized discipline, verification engineers must understand scan chains, ATPG, MBIST, LBIST, boundary scan, JTAG, DFT insertion, test coverage, and DFT verification — because DFT logic must itself be verified, and DFT features often interact with functional logic in unexpected ways.

## 39.1 What is DFT?

DFT adds hardware structures to a design specifically to improve testability during manufacturing. After fabrication, every die is tested to detect manufacturing defects — shorts, opens, stuck-at faults, bridging faults, delay faults, and cell defects. Without DFT, many manufacturing defects would be undetectable.

## 39.2 Why DFT Matters to Verification Engineers

DFT logic interacts with functional logic. Scan chains connect through functional flip-flops. JTAG controls test modes that affect system behavior. MBIST takes memory offline for testing. Verification must ensure that DFT features function correctly, do not disturb functional operation when inactive, and recover cleanly after test.

## 39.3 Fault Models

**Stuck-at-0:** a net permanently at logic 0. **Stuck-at-1:** a net permanently at logic 1. **Transition delay:** a net that transitions but too slowly. **Bridging:** two nets inadvertently connected. **Cell defect:** an internal cell failure. Each fault model requires different test patterns.

## 39.4 Scan Chains

Scan chains convert flip-flops into a shift register for test:

```text
Scan-In → FF1 → FF2 → FF3 → ... → FFN → Scan-Out
```

In **scan mode**, data is shifted in serially, applied to the circuit, and the response is shifted out and compared against expected values. Scan provides controllability and observability of every flip-flop.

## 39.5 Scan Architecture

```text
Test Controller → Scan Enable → All FFs → Scan Chain → Scan Out
```

Key signals: `scan_en` (enables scan mode), `scan_in`, `scan_out`, `test_mode`. Functional flip-flops become scan cells with a 2-to-1 mux at the D input — functional data or scan data.

## 39.6 Scan Cell

```systemverilog
// Conceptual scan cell
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) q <= '0;
    else        q <= scan_en ? scan_in : func_d;
end
```

When `scan_en` is high, the flip-flop becomes part of the shift register. When low, it operates functionally.

## 39.7 ATPG — Automatic Test Pattern Generation

ATPG tools (Synopsys TetraMAX, Mentor FastScan, Cadence Encounter Test) automatically generate test patterns that detect specific faults:

```text
Fault List → ATPG Algorithm → Test Patterns → Fault Coverage Report
```

Target: >99% stuck-at fault coverage for production silicon.

## 39.8 Scan Insertion

DFT tools automatically insert scan cells, stitch chains, add test ports, and generate DFT netlists:

```text
RTL → Synthesis → DFT Insertion → Scan-Stitched Netlist → ATPG
```

Verification must validate both the pre-insertion RTL and the post-insertion netlist.

## 39.9 Memory BIST (MBIST)

```text
MBIST Controller → Address/Data/Control → Memory → Read-back → Pass/Fail
```

MBIST runs algorithms (MARCH C, MARCH X, MATS+, checkerboard) inside the chip to test memories without external pattern generation. Verification: BIST enable, algorithm execution, pass/fail reporting, and interaction with functional logic.

## 39.10 Logic BIST (LBIST)

LBIST tests logic gates using on-chip pattern generation (LFSR) and signature analysis (MISR):

```text
LFSR → Stimulus → CUT → Response → MISR → Signature → Compare → Pass/Fail
```

LBIST reduces external tester time for complex logic blocks.

## 39.11 Boundary Scan (JTAG — IEEE 1149.1)

JTAG provides serial access to device I/Os through a Test Access Port (TAP):

```text
TDI → TAP Controller → Boundary Scan Register → TDO
TCK, TMS (control)
TRST (optional reset)
```

Applications: board-level test, IC connectivity test, memory programming, debug access, firmware download.

## 39.12 TAP Controller FSM

The JTAG TAP controller is a 16-state FSM driven by TMS:

```text
Test-Logic-Reset → Run-Test/Idle → Select-DR → Capture-DR →
Shift-DR → Exit1-DR → Pause-DR → Exit2-DR → Update-DR
```

Verification: every state, every transition, TMS sequences, reset, TRST.

## 39.13 JTAG Instructions

Common instructions: BYPASS, IDCODE, EXTEST, INTEST, SAMPLE/PRELOAD, RUNBIST. Verification: correct execution of each instruction, correct response in TDO, interaction with functional logic.

## 39.14 DFT Verification Scope

Verification engineers are responsible for:
- Scan chain continuity (all FFs connected, correct length)
- Scan enable/disable behavior (no functional disturbance)
- MBIST execution and reporting
- LBIST execution and signature comparison
- JTAG TAP FSM correctness
- JTAG instruction execution
- DFT mode isolation from functional mode
- Recovery after DFT test completion

## 39.15 Scan Chain Verification

```text
Assert scan_en → Shift known pattern → Read scan_out →
Compare against expected → Verify chain length → Release scan_en
```

Verification confirms every flip-flop is reachable, correctly stitched, and returns the correct value.

## 39.16 DFT Mode Isolation

DFT test mode must never disturb functional operation when deasserted. Verification:
- Apply DFT test sequence
- Return to functional mode
- Confirm all registers contain correct post-reset values
- Confirm all functional interfaces operate normally
- Confirm no residual DFT state affects functional behavior

## 39.17 DFT Interaction with Power Management

DFT and power management interact significantly — scan testing may require all power domains active. Verification must confirm correct power sequencing before DFT test, correct isolation during MBIST, and correct recovery.

## 39.18 DFT Interaction with CDC

Scan chains cross clock domains and may violate standard CDC rules intentionally. CDC lint tools must be configured to waive these known DFT violations. Verification must confirm functional CDC paths are not affected by DFT insertion.

## 39.19 Fault Coverage Metrics

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| Stuck-at fault coverage | >99% |
| Transition delay coverage | >95% |
| ATPG pattern count | Minimized for test time |
| Memory test coverage | 100% |
| Scan chain length | Balanced across chains |

## 39.20 DFT Signoff Checklist

Scan chains verified, ATPG coverage target achieved, MBIST verified, LBIST verified, JTAG TAP verified, DFT mode isolation confirmed, power interaction verified, CDC interaction documented, test time estimated, and DFT report included in tapeout package.

## 39.21 Verification vs. DFT Engineering

| Functional Verification | DFT Engineering |
|---|---|
| Proves design intent | Proves manufacturing quality |
| Simulation-based | ATPG and BIST-based |
| Pre-silicon | Post-silicon manufacturing |
| Finds design bugs | Finds manufacturing defects |
| RTL and gate-level | Gate-level and silicon |

Both disciplines are required for a complete quality assurance strategy.

## 39.22 Chapter Summary

DFT adds hardware that enables manufacturing test of every fabricated die. Verification engineers must understand scan, ATPG, MBIST, LBIST, JTAG, DFT insertion, and the interactions between DFT and functional logic, power management, and CDC. DFT features must be verified as rigorously as any other functional block.

## Engineering Exercise

For a block with scan, MBIST, and JTAG: (1) verify scan chain continuity; (2) verify scan enable/disable isolation; (3) execute MBIST and verify pass/fail reporting; (4) verify JTAG TAP FSM completeness; (5) execute BYPASS and IDCODE instructions; (6) verify DFT mode isolation from functional mode; (7) verify recovery after DFT test; (8) verify power-domain interaction with DFT; (9) document CDC waivers for DFT scan paths; (10) produce a DFT verification signoff report.

## The AVIK Studio Golden Rule

**A design that passes functional verification but fails manufacturing test ships a defective product. Verify DFT as rigorously as functional behavior — because the quality of the silicon your customers receive depends on both.**
